laws.act: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Mandates that a month-to-month lease termination notice must be served in writing with at least 15 days notice.
laws.details: Requires a minimum of 15 days notice for terminating a monthly tenancy of immovable property. The notice must be in writing, signed by the party, and served personally or by post. Failure to provide a full 15-day notice makes any subsequent eviction suit legally void.
remedies: Check the date of service of the eviction notice.
Verify if a full 15 days is allowed before the vacate date.
Consult an advocate to draft a reply highlighting any timing defects.

laws.act: Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.scope: Rights and Liabilities of Landlord and Tenant
laws.summary: Defines mutual rights and duties, including landlord's duty to maintain property and tenant's duty to pay rent.
laws.details: Details that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the landlord is bound to disclose material defects in the property. The tenant is obligated to pay rent at proper times and maintain the property in good condition, normal wear and tear excepted.
remedies: Request repairs for material property defects.
Keep evidence of regular rent payment transactions.
Send a written notice if the landlord fails to make basic structure repairs.

laws.act: Section 12 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
laws.summary: Restricts landlords from evicting tenants if they regularly pay the standard rent and permitted increases.
laws.details: A landlord shall not be entitled to the recovery of possession of any premises so long as the tenant pays, or is ready and willing to pay, the amount of standard rent and permitted increases, and observes the other conditions of the tenancy.
remedies: Pay any rent arrears within 90 days of landlord demand.
Deposit standard rent in court if landlord refuses acceptance.
Obtain printed receipts for all rent transactions.

laws.act: Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
laws.scope: Grounds for Landlord Recovery of Possession
laws.summary: Outlines specific grounds like personal necessity or non-payment of rent for recovering premises.
laws.details: Restricts recovery of possession except on specific statutory grounds such as: tenant defaulted in rent for two consecutive months, subletting without written consent, or landlord requires premises for personal residential necessity.
remedies: Dispute arbitrary claims of personal necessity.
Provide proof of written consent for any subletting arrangement.
Clear dues within one month of receiving a legal demand notice.

laws.act: Section 21 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
laws.summary: Requires landlords to keep premises in good tenantable repair, failing which tenants can make repairs and deduct costs.
laws.details: Every landlord shall keep the premises in good and tenantable repair. If the landlord neglects to make repairs after receiving fifteen days notice in writing, the tenant may make such repairs and deduct the expenses from the rent, capped at one-fourth of the annual rent.
remedies: Send a written 15-day notice demanding essential structural repairs.
Execute repairs locally if ignored, keeping all bill receipts.
Deduct up to 25% of annual rent to offset repair expenses.

laws.act: Section 56 of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999
laws.summary: Validates the receipt of key-money (Pugree) or premium as part of tenancy transactions.
laws.details: Declares that it shall be lawful for a tenant to claim or receive any sum in consideration of the relinquishment, transfer or assignment of his tenancy of any premises, validating traditional Pugree transfer premiums.
remedies: Draft a formal tripartite Pugree transfer agreement.
Pay the landlord's consent fee (usually 33% of transfer premium).
File a lawsuit if landlord refuses consent arbitrarily.

laws.act: Section 18 of the Real Estate Regulation and Development Act (RERA), 2016
laws.scope: Return of Amount and Compensation for Delayed Possession
laws.summary: Entitles allottees to a full refund with interest if the promoter fails to give possession on time.
laws.details: Mandates that if the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment in accordance with the agreement for sale, he shall be liable to return the amount received with interest and compensation if the allottee wishes to withdraw.
remedies: File a claim before the RERA Adjudicating Officer.
Demand refund of principal amount along with prescribed delay interest.
Apply for interest on delay even if you choose to remain in the project.

laws.act: Section 31 of the RERA Act, 2016
laws.summary: Allows any aggrieved person to file a complaint for RERA violations against builders or agents.
laws.details: Provides that any aggrieved person may file a complaint with the RERA Authority or the Adjudicating Officer for any violation or contravention of the provisions of this Act or the rules and regulations made thereunder.
remedies: File Form M online on the state RERA portal.
Attach builder agreements and receipt vouchers.
Represent your case personally or via an advocate before the authority.

laws.act: Section 19 of the RERA Act, 2016
laws.summary: Details the rights of home buyers to obtain information on sanitations, layouts, and timelines.
laws.details: Home buyers (allottees) have the right to obtain information on stage-wise completion plans, water, sanitation, and electricity. The allottee is also duty-bound to make timely stage payments as per the sale agreement.
remedies: Demand structural layout plans from the builder.
Withhold payment if stage completion certificate is not shown.
Pay interest on genuine payment delays if demanded as per RERA terms.

laws.act: Section 11 of the RERA Act, 2016
laws.summary: Requires builders to register advertisements, update project details quarterly, and provide occupancy certificates.
laws.details: The builder (promoter) must upload project details on the RERA website quarterly. The promoter is responsible for all obligations under the sale agreement, obtaining leasehold titles, and providing occupancy/completion certificates.
remedies: Verify project registration status on RERA website.
Inspect quarterly progress updates of the towers.
Refuse possession until builder provides a valid Occupancy Certificate (OC).

laws.act: Section 12 of the Tamil Nadu Regulation of Landlords and Tenants Act, 2017
laws.summary: Mandates that all tenancy agreements must be registered in writing with the Rent Authority.
laws.details: No landlord shall let out and no tenant shall take on rent any premises except by an agreement in writing. This agreement must be registered with the Rent Authority within ninety days of execution.
remedies: Draft a clear, written tenancy contract.
Register the agreement on the state tenancy portal within 90 days.
Keep the registration ID for any future rent tribunal filings.

laws.act: Section 21 of the Tamil Nadu Landlord Tenant Act, 2017
laws.summary: Limits eviction of tenants to statutory defaults like rent non-payment, damage, or misuse.
laws.details: Allows a landlord to apply to the Rent Court for recovery of possession only on specific defaults: failure to pay rent for two months, misuse of premises causing nuisance, or structural alteration without written consent.
remedies: File written replies disputing false claims of nuisance.
Provide proof of regular rent payments to dismiss eviction.
Demand compensation if landlord cuts off water/power services illegally.

laws.act: Section 15 of the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999
laws.summary: Restricts the right of tenancy inheritance to direct dependent relatives upon tenant's death.
laws.details: In the event of the death of a tenant, the right of tenancy shall devolve for a limited period on the surviving spouse, children, or parents who were ordinarily residing with the tenant as members of the family.
remedies: Apply for name transfer in tenancy records as a legal heir.
Submit proof of co-residence (Aadhaar/Voter ID) with deceased tenant.
Clear any unpaid rent arrears immediately to prevent eviction.

laws.act: Section 27 of the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999
laws.summary: Allows tenants to deposit rent directly with the court if the landlord refuses to accept it.
laws.details: Where the landlord refuses to accept rent or deliver a printed receipt, the tenant may deposit the rent with the Rent Controller after serving a written notice to the landlord.
remedies: Send a written warning notice via registered post.
Apply to deposit monthly rent with the Rent Controller.
Use deposit receipts as proof in eviction defense cases.

laws.act: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Defines a lease as a transfer of right to enjoy property for a specified time in consideration of price/rent.
laws.details: Establishes that a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for a certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised.
remedies: Ensure the lease document clearly specifies duration.
Verify rent and security deposit refund parameters.
Incorporate lock-in period terms to prevent premature eviction.

laws.act: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Imposes criminal liability and up to 2 years prison for cheque bounces due to insufficient funds.
laws.details: Deals with dishonor of cheques for insufficiency of funds. Payee must send a demand notice within 30 days of dishonor. The drawer gets 15 days from notice receipt to pay the amount. Failure to pay within 15 days allows filing a criminal lawsuit within 30 days.
remedies: Settle the bounced cheque amount within 15 days of notice receipt.
Verify if the bank return memo matches account records.
Engage legal counsel to draft a response if cheque was given as security.

laws.act: Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Presumes that a bounced cheque was issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt.
laws.details: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.
remedies: Gather clear documentation proving the debt was already discharged.
Submit agreements proving the cheque was security and not for active debt.
Cross-examine the complainant to shake the legal liability presumption.

laws.act: Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Holds company directors and officers personally liable for corporate cheque bounces.
laws.details: If the person committing an offence under section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business, shall be deemed guilty.
remedies: Identify directors who were active in daily company conduct.
Resign directors can show they had no knowledge of transaction.
Draft company responses separately from director liabilities.

laws.act: Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Limits filing of Section 138 complaints to within 1 month after the 15-day notice period ends.
laws.details: Restricts courts from taking cognizance of Section 138 offences unless a written complaint is made by the payee within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises (15 days after notice receipt).
remedies: Verify if the criminal complaint was filed within the 30-day window.
File a condonation of delay application if the filing deadline was missed.
Challenge time-barred complaints to dismiss the criminal case.

laws.act: Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.summary: Allows banks to issue 60-day demand notices to default borrowers to clear secured debts.
laws.details: Enables secured creditors (banks) to enforce security interests without court intervention. Banks issue a 60-day demand notice (Sec 13(2)) to the default borrower. If ignored, the bank can take symbolic or physical possession (Sec 13(4)) of the property.
remedies: Submit formal written objections/representations (Sec 13(3A)) within 15 days.
Pay the overdue balance within 60 days to prevent property possession.
Verify if the asset classification (NPA) matches RBI guidelines.

laws.act: Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.summary: Empowers banks to request Magistrate assistance to take physical control of default properties.
laws.details: Where the possession of any secured asset is required to be taken by the bank, they may request the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or District Magistrate (DM) within whose jurisdiction the asset is located to take possession.
remedies: Verify if the bank filed a valid affidavit confirming loan terms.
Check if magistrate notice was served to occupants.
File an urgent appeal to stay physical dispossession.

laws.act: Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.scope: Right to Appeal in Debts Recovery Tribunal
laws.summary: Entitles borrowers to appeal bank enforcement actions within 45 days in the DRT.
laws.details: Any person (including the borrower) aggrieved by bank measures under Section 13(4) may make an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) within forty-five days from the date on which such measures had been taken.
remedies: File a Securitisation Application (SA) in the DRT within 45 days.
Challenge procedural errors in the possession notice.
Obtain an interim stay on property auctions by depositing a fraction of the debt.

laws.act: Section 19 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.summary: Governs formal recovery lawsuits filed by banks in the DRT and defendant reply timelines.
laws.details: Specifies procedures for financial banks to file applications in the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) for debt recovery. The defendant receives summons and must file a Written Statement of defense within 30 days (extendable by 15 days).
remedies: File a detailed Written Reply Statement within 30 days of receiving summons.
Verify interest calculations, compoundings, and penal charges.
File counter-claims if the bank caused monetary losses to your business.

laws.act: Section 20 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.scope: Appeals to Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal
laws.summary: Allows appealing DRT orders to the Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within 30 days.
laws.details: Any person aggrieved by an order made by the DRT may prefer an appeal to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within thirty days from the date of receipt of the order.
remedies: File a formal appeal petition to the DRAT within 30 days.
Submit certified copies of the DRT order.
Deposit the mandatory pre-deposit amount to let the appeal proceed.

laws.act: Section 21 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.scope: Deposit of Debt Amount for Appeal
laws.summary: Mandates pre-depositing 50% of the debt before the DRAT will hear the appeal.
laws.details: No appeal by a debtor shall be entertained by the DRAT unless the debtor deposits fifty percent of the debt amount determined by the DRT. The DRAT may reduce this to not less than twenty-five percent.
remedies: Request a waiver of pre-deposit down to 25% by filing an application.
Pay the pre-deposit amount via demand draft to the DRAT Registry.
Submit arguments of financial hardship to justify a reduced deposit.

laws.act: Section 25 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.summary: Details methods Recovery Officers use to recover dues, including selling property or arrest.
laws.details: Allows Recovery Officers to recover the debt specified in the certificate by attachment and sale of movable/immovable property, arrest of the defendant, and appointing a receiver to manage properties.
remedies: Dispute the attachment of personal properties not mortgaged.
Request installment options to pay off the certificate amount.
Apply to stay arrest warrants by showing cooperative asset disclosures.

laws.act: Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Allows banks to trigger corporate insolvency proceedings in NCLT for loan defaults.
laws.details: A financial creditor (bank/lender) may file an application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) when a default has occurred.
remedies: File a written response disputing the occurrence of default.
Check if the default amount meets the threshold limit (INR 1 Crore).
Settle the outstanding claim through settlement agreements before admission.

laws.act: Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Enables vendors/suppliers to initiate NCLT insolvency after serving a 10-day demand notice.
laws.details: After the expiry of ten days from the delivery of the demand notice under Section 8, if the operational creditor does not receive payment or notice of dispute, they may file an application in the NCLT to initiate insolvency.
remedies: Serve a reply notice within 10 days highlighting pre-existing quality disputes.
Submit proof of payment transactions.
Settle vendor payments to prevent business insolvency admission.

laws.act: Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Declares a freeze on all lawsuits, recovery actions, and foreclosure measures during insolvency.
laws.details: Requires the Adjudicating Authority to declare a moratorium prohibiting: the institution or continuation of suits, enforcement of any security interest (SARFAESI), or recovery of any property by an owner or lessor.
remedies: Apply to stay active civil court/DRT recovery trials.
Block bank possession notices (Sec 13(4)) while moratorium is active.
Continue operational business transactions under the Resolution Professional.

laws.act: Section 31 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
laws.scope: Submission of Accounts and Balance Sheets
laws.summary: Requires banks to publish audited balance sheets, ensuring public transparency.
laws.details: Mandates that every banking company must prepare and submit audited accounts and balance sheets to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) within three months from the end of the period to which they relate.
remedies: Request audited financial sheets for corporate loan matching.
Audit bank interest statements against published schedules.
File complaints with the banking ombudsman for illegal accounts manipulations.

laws.act: Section 2(9) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Guarantees rights including protection against hazardous goods, information access, and competitive pricing.
laws.details: Defines core consumer rights: right to be protected against marketing of goods hazardous to life; right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, and price; right to be assured competitive prices; and right to seek redressal against unfair exploitation.
remedies: File written complaints on the National Consumer Helpline.
Demand product specifications and quality certifications.
Refuse purchasing items lacking price/manufacturing date labels.

laws.act: Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Allows consumers to file formal complaints before the District Commission regarding defects.
laws.details: Allows a consumer, recognized consumer association, or Central Authority to file a complaint with the District Commission regarding defective goods, deficient services, overcharging, or unfair trade practices.
remedies: Draft a formal complaint listing purchase receipts and communications.
File the case online using the E-Daakhil portal.
Serve the required pre-complaint legal notice to the vendor.

laws.act: Section 38 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Outlines response timelines for opposite parties and laboratory testing procedures.
laws.details: Requires the District Commission to refer a copy of the admitted complaint to the opposite party, directing them to file their version within thirty days (extendable by fifteen days). Allows testing in designated laboratories if product defects are hard to verify.
remedies: File opposite party reply statement within 30 days of receiving notice.
Request lab testing for industrial / chemical defects.
Present arguments within the commission's hearing schedule.

laws.act: Section 39 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Authorizes commissions to order replacements, refunds, or compensation for losses.
laws.details: Empowers the commission, upon finding defects or deficiencies, to order the seller to: remove the defect, replace the goods, return the price paid, or pay compensation for any loss/injury suffered by the consumer.
remedies: Request execution of commission orders if the company delays compliance.
Demand refund of price along with reasonable interest.
Claim compensation for mental harassment and litigation costs.

laws.act: Section 47 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Sets pecuniary limits for appealing District orders or filing directly in the State Commission.
laws.details: Details that the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of goods/services paid exceeds INR 50 Lakhs but does not exceed INR 2 Crores, and to hear appeals against District Commission orders.
remedies: File appeals to the State Commission within 45 days of District order.
File high-value complaints directly to the State Commission.
Deposit 50% of the ordered amount before filing an appeal as required.

laws.act: Section 58 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Handles consumer complaints exceeding INR 2 Crores and appeals against State orders.
laws.details: The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) has jurisdiction for complaints where the value paid exceeds INR 2 Crores, and has appellate power over State Commission orders.
remedies: File direct petitions to NCDRC for high-value corporate defaults.
File second appeals against State orders within 30 days.
Submit case briefs directly at the NCDRC registry in New Delhi.

laws.act: Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Defines misleading advertisements, false quality claims, and refusal to issue receipts as illegal.
laws.details: Defines an unfair trade practice as a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting sales, adopts any unfair method or deceptive practice including: falsely representing goods, making misleading statements, or refusing to issue cash memos/receipts.
remedies: Report vendors refusing to print retail tax bills.
Submit screenshots of misleading web listings as evidence.
Claim damages for bait-and-switch pricing tactics.

laws.act: Section 2(28) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Imposes penalties on manufacturers and endorsers for publishing false product claims.
laws.details: An advertisement is misleading if it falsely describes a product, guarantees performance without scientific proof, or contains representation that is likely to deceive the consumer.
remedies: File complaints against misleading endorsements to the CCPA (Central Authority).
Demand proof of performance claims from manufacturers.
Refuse purchases based on unverified miracle cure ads.

laws.act: Section 84 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Holds manufacturers liable for design defects, manufacturing errors, or lack of warnings.
laws.details: A product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action if the product contains a manufacturing defect, is defective in design, deviates from specifications, or does not contain adequate instructions on correct usage.
remedies: File product liability suits for injuries caused by design flaws.
Document product failure with photos and user manuals.
Request replacement of all defective batches from the vendor.

laws.act: Section 85 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Holds service providers liable for poor quality, negligence, or lack of safety warnings.
laws.details: A product service provider shall be liable in a product liability action if the service was faulty or deficient, they withheld adequate instructions, or they did not conform to express warranty terms.
remedies: File negligence claims for faulty electronic/mechanical repairs.
Submit warranty card copies proving service agreements.
Seek recovery for damages caused by poor service executions.

laws.act: Section 86 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Holds retail sellers liable if they altered the product, made independent warranties, or cannot identify the manufacturer.
laws.details: A product seller who is not a manufacturer shall be liable if they exercised control over design/packaging, altered the product, or if the manufacturer is not subject to law in India.
remedies: Settle claims with local retail sellers if foreign manufacturers cannot be reached.
Dispute altered packages sold in retail outlets.
Document seller's verbal performance promises.

laws.act: Section 90 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
laws.summary: Limits trial of offences under this Act to Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrates.
laws.details: No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try any offence punishable under this Act, ensuring formal judicial oversight.
remedies: Verify that criminal complaints under this Act are filed in competent Magistrate courts.
Challenge prosecutions initiated in improper forums.
File appeals against Magistrate orders in District Session Courts.

laws.act: Section 5 of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Act, 2016
laws.summary: Regulates the printing of ISI/BIS quality marks on consumer products.
laws.details: Requires manufacturers of notified items (like helmets, cylinders, electronic items) to conform to BIS standards and print standard marks. Selling fake certified goods constitutes an offense.
remedies: Verify the ISI/BIS registration number online on the BIS app.
File complaints against duplicate goods using standard marks.
Refuse purchases of non-certified helmets or electricals.

laws.act: Section 12 of the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006
laws.summary: Requires food business operators to provide written warranty on food safety.
laws.details: Mandates that no food manufacturer or distributor shall sell food items without giving a written warranty regarding the purity and safety of the food to the purchaser/retailer.
remedies: Demand food purity test reports from manufacturers.
File complaints to the local Food Safety Officer for contaminated purchases.
Keep restaurant bills showing food items ordered.

laws.act: Section 40 of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009
laws.summary: Prohibits the sale of pre-packaged commodities lacking standard weight, price, or manufacturer labels.
laws.details: No person shall manufacture, pack, import, or sell any pre-packaged commodity unless such package bears declarations including net weight, manufacturing date, retail sale price (MRP), and consumer care details.
remedies: Refuse paying more than the printed Maximum Retail Price (MRP).
Report packages lacking manufacturer details or weight prints.
File legal claims for underweight packed packages.

laws.act: Section 56 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.summary: Prohibits power disconnection unless a clear 15-day written warning is served to the consumer.
laws.details: Restricts utility companies from cutting off electricity supply unless the consumer has neglected payment of dues for a period of fifteen clear days. The warning must be in writing and served to the consumer.
remedies: Verify if you received 15 clear days notice in writing before power cuts.
Pay the undisputed base balance to prevent service disconnection.
File complaints to the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF) for sudden cuts.

laws.act: Section 42 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.summary: Mandates electricity distribution companies to establish a forum (CGRF) for customer complaints.
laws.details: Every distribution licensee must establish a forum for redressal of grievances of the consumers in accordance with guidelines as specified by the State Commission. Aggrieved consumers can appeal to the Electricity Ombudsman.
remedies: File complaints to the CGRF regarding billing errors or faulty meters.
File appeals to the Electricity Ombudsman if CGRF rejects your claims.
Obtain grievance case registration IDs for tracking.

laws.act: Section 43 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.scope: Duty to Supply Electricity on Request
laws.summary: Requires power utilities to provide power connection within 1 month of receiving an application.
laws.details: Mandates that every distribution licensee shall, on an application by the owner or occupier of any premises, give supply of electricity to such premises, within one month after receipt of the application.
remedies: Submit applications with ownership/occupancy proof (Sale Deed/Lease).
Claim penalty charges (up to INR 1,000 per day of delay) if supply is delayed beyond 30 days.
File petitions to the state electricity commission for denial of service.

laws.act: Section 50 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.summary: Requires state commissions to publish a supply code detailing connection and meter reading rules.
laws.details: Requires the State Commission to specify an Electricity Supply Code to provide for recovery of electricity charges, intervals of billing, installation of meters, and conditions of supply.
remedies: Verify billing intervals match the published State Supply Code.
Demand annual tests of connection meters to check accuracy.
Dispute arbitrary security deposit hikes not matching code formulas.

laws.act: Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.scope: Assessment of Unauthorized Use of Electricity
laws.summary: Outlines assessment and penalty rules if a consumer is found using power unauthorizedly.
laws.details: If on inspection of any premises, the assessing officer comes to the conclusion that such person is indulging in unauthorized use of electricity, he shall provisionally assess the electricity charges at twice the normal rate.
remedies: Submit written objections to the provisional assessment within 15 days.
File appeals to the Appellate Authority after depositing 50% of the assessed amount.
Verify if the inspection was executed by an authorized officer with valid IDs.

laws.act: Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.summary: Imposes criminal penalties for tapping lines, tampering meters, or bypassing connections.
laws.details: Provides that whoever dishonestly taps overhead lines, tampers with meters, or damages equipment to abstract energy shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine.
remedies: Ensure meters are sealed and show no physical tampering.
Verify if power line tapping claims have solid photo/video evidence.
File bail petitions immediately if criminal FIRs are filed.

laws.act: Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003
laws.summary: Imposes penalties on utility companies that violate state commission orders.
laws.details: If any licensee fails to comply with any direction of the Commission, they shall pay a penalty not exceeding one lakh rupees for each contravention, and additional fines for continuing defaults.
remedies: Report utility companies violating grid codes to the State Commission.
Apply for compensation for continuous load-sheddings.
Demand compliance files from regional substation offices.

laws.act: Section 24 of the Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
laws.scope: Prohibition on Pollution of Streams and Wells
laws.summary: Bans discharging toxic or polluting sewage directly into water bodies.
laws.details: No person shall knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter determined in accordance with standards laid down by the State Board to enter into any stream or well or sewer.
remedies: File complaints to the State Pollution Control Board for factory discharge.
Verify if the local municipal plant has water filtration setups.
Obtain water quality test reports from public health labs.

laws.act: Section 25 of the Water Act, 1974
laws.summary: Requires consent from the State Board before setting up new outlet sewers.
laws.details: No person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board, establish or take any steps to establish any industry, operation or process, or any treatment and disposal system which is likely to discharge sewage.
remedies: Verify if nearby factories have valid 'Consent to Establish' certificates.
Report unauthorized sewage construction lines.
File public petitions against dumping sewers close to residential zones.

laws.act: Section 21 of the Air (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
laws.summary: Requires prior consent from the State Pollution Board to operate industrial plants.
laws.details: Restricts operation of any industrial plant in an air pollution control area unless previous consent of the State Board has been obtained. Violations invite heavy penalties and closure.
remedies: Request copies of 'Consent to Operate' from polluting neighborhood units.
Report emission standard violations with air quality tracking graphs.
Apply for closure orders of unlicensed brick kilns/mixers.

laws.act: Section 15 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
laws.scope: Penalty for Contravention of Environment Rules
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 5 years and heavy fines for violating ecological rules.
laws.details: Imposes strict criminal liability for failing to comply with directions issued under this Act. Violations are punishable with imprisonment up to five years, or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or both.
remedies: File National Green Tribunal (NGT) petitions for local waste burnings.
Report illegal hazardous waste dumping yards.
Document ecological damages with geo-tagged photos.

laws.act: Section 19 of the Municipal Corporation Act
laws.summary: Empowers Municipalities to issue notices to landowners to clean choked drains.
laws.details: Authorizes the municipal commissioner to serve written notices to owners of buildings requiring them to repair, clear, or construct proper toilet septic pipes and sewage lines within a specified timeframe.
remedies: Send letters to municipal wards for clearing blocked community drains.
Verify if warning notices list clear timelines.
Dispute arbitrary fines if drainage choke is outside property boundaries.

laws.act: Section 234 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957
laws.summary: Outlines rules for obtaining water connections and installing water meters.
laws.details: Regulates the supply of water for domestic purposes, installation of water meters, and penalties for wasting water or using illegal sub-pumps on main municipal lines.
remedies: Apply for name updates in domestic water bills.
Report usage of high-power sub-pumps by neighbors during dry seasons.
Challenge inflated utility water bills based on average meter readings.

laws.act: Section 313 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957
laws.scope: Layout Plans of Land and Building Notices
laws.summary: Prohibits construction of layouts or buildings without municipal plan sanction.
laws.details: Mandates that any person intending to lay out a new private street or construct buildings must submit detailed layout plans to the Commissioner for approval. Unauthorized constructions are liable to demolition.
remedies: Obtain municipal sanctioned building plan copies before purchase.
Verify if demolition notices allow a 15-day cure period.
File civil court injunction suits to halt illegal municipal demolitions.

laws.act: Section 4 of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005
laws.summary: Requires government departments to proactively publish key data, including directories and budgets.
laws.details: Every public authority shall maintain all its records cataloged and indexed, and publish details of its organization, functions, directories, salary scales, and project subsidy allocations.
remedies: File formal online RTI applications for delayed public project details.
Inspect regional utility project expenditure sheets.
Challenge vague responses from Public Information Officers (PIOs).

laws.act: Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) / BNS 356
laws.summary: Defines defamation as false spoken/written words damaging a citizen's reputation, with 10 exceptions.
laws.details: Defines defamation. Outlines that making or publishing any imputation intending to harm the reputation of a person constitutes an offense, subject to 10 exceptions (such as imputation of truth for public good, or public conduct of public servants).
remedies: Check if the statements fall under the 10 statutory exceptions.
Draft responses to legal notices denying malicious intent.
Keep records of published source materials to prove truth/public good.

laws.act: Section 500 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) / BNS 356
laws.summary: Imposes simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both for defamation.
laws.details: Specifies punishment for criminal defamation. Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
remedies: File criminal quash petitions in the High Court if cases are vexatious.
Engage legal representation for magistrate hearings.
Propose mutual retraction and apology letters to settle disputes outside court.

laws.act: Section 66A of the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000
laws.summary: Deals with sending offensive messages electronically (Note: struck down by Supreme Court).
laws.details: Previously punished sending offensive or annoying messages using computer resource. Landmark judgment 'Shreya Singhal v. Union of India' struck this section down as unconstitutional. No FIR can be legally registered under this section.
remedies: Demand immediate dismissal of any FIR citing Section 66A.
Reference the Supreme Court Shreya Singhal judgment in court replies.
File counter-petitions for harassment against police misuse of struck-down laws.

laws.act: Section 66C of the IT Act, 2000
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 3 years and INR 1 Lakh fine for fraudulent use of digital signatures/IDs.
laws.details: Punishes identity theft. Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years.
remedies: Report hacked accounts to the Cyber Crime cell immediately.
Block compromised digital signatures.
Submit bank transaction logs and IP login trace history in identity theft defense.

laws.act: Section 66D of the IT Act, 2000
laws.scope: Cheating by Personation using Computer Resource
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 3 years for cheating by pretending to be someone else online.
laws.details: Punishes cheating by personation. Whoever by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years.
remedies: File cyber cell complaints for fake social media profiles.
Verify banking representative IDs before sharing transaction OTPs.
Track email headers to confirm sender domain authenticity in phishing cases.

laws.act: Section 66E of the IT Act, 2000
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 3 years for publishing private images of individuals without consent.
laws.details: Punishes violation of privacy. Whoever, intentionally captures, publishes or transmits the image of a private area of any person without his or her consent, shall be punished with imprisonment up to three years or with fine.
remedies: File urgent injunction requests to pull down non-consensual private images.
Submit platform abuse notices on Google/Meta/Twitter to block links.
Register cyber cell complaints with IP logins and messaging screenshots.

laws.act: Section 67 of the IT Act, 2000
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 3 years for publishing sexually explicit content online.
laws.details: Punishes publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form. First conviction carries prison up to three years and fine up to five lakh rupees; subsequent convictions invite heavier sentences.
remedies: Audit online content uploads to ensure compliance with censorship laws.
Submit written representations proving content has artistic or scientific merit.
Engage legal counsel to secure anticipatory bail if accused falsely.

laws.act: Section 72 of the IT Act, 2000
laws.summary: Imposes prison up to 2 years for government/system administrators sharing private records without consent.
laws.details: Punishes breach of confidentiality. If any person who has secured access to any electronic record, book, register or document without consent discloses such information, they shall be liable to prison up to two years.
remedies: Report system administrators sharing private chat history logs or customer profiles.
File civil suits for corporate breach of confidentiality.
Audit server login logs to trace unauthorized record accesses.

laws.act: Section 43 of the IT Act, 2000
laws.scope: Penalty for Damage to Computer and Network
laws.summary: Imposes heavy compensation penalties for downloading data or introducing viruses without permission.
laws.details: If any person, without permission of the owner, accesses a computer, downloads or extracts data, introduces a computer contaminant or virus, or damages data, they shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the affected person.
remedies: File claims before the Adjudicating Officer under the IT Act for compensation.
Document data loss with server audit reports and technician logs.
Establish firewall protocols to prove secure database ownership.

laws.act: Section 43A of the IT Act, 2000
laws.scope: Compensation for Failure to Protect Sensitive Data
laws.summary: Holds corporate bodies liable to pay unlimited damages for failing to secure private user databases.
laws.details: Where a body corporate, possessing, dealing or handling any sensitive personal data in a computer resource, is negligent in maintaining reasonable security practices, resulting in wrongful loss/gain, they shall be liable to pay damages.
remedies: File class-action style compensation complaints for corporate database leaks.
Verify if the target company follows ISO/IEC 27001 security standards.
Document financial losses resulting from identity leakage.

laws.act: Section 4 of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023
laws.summary: Restricts corporate processing of personal data to lawful purposes with explicit consent.
laws.details: A person may process personal data of a Data Principal only in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and for a lawful purpose for which the Data Principal has given her consent.
remedies: Request standard data processing disclosure declarations from mobile apps.
Withhold consent for processing unrelated to core services.
File notices demanding deletion of data collected without lawful basis.

laws.act: Section 5 of the DPDP Act, 2023
laws.summary: Mandates companies to serve written notices detailing what data is collected and why.
laws.details: Every request for consent shall be accompanied or preceded by a notice containing: the personal data to be processed, the purpose, and the manner in which the Data Principal can exercise her right to withdraw consent.
remedies: Read the mandatory data collection notice popped up by applications.
Verify if the notice lists English and regional languages option.
Identify the designated Data Protection Officer's contact details.

laws.act: Section 6 of the DPDP Act, 2023
laws.summary: Mandates that data consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional, and withdrawable.
laws.details: Consent given by the Data Principal shall be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action. The Principal has the right to withdraw her consent at any time.
remedies: Withdraw data sharing consent through corporate portal settings.
Refuse check-box agreements that bundle unnecessary personal permissions.
Keep copies of data processing approvals.

laws.act: Section 13 of the DPDP Act, 2023
laws.summary: Entitles citizens to file complaints regarding privacy violations directly with the Data Fiduciary.
laws.details: A Data Principal shall have the right to register a grievance with a Data Fiduciary regarding any act or omission of such Fiduciary in relation to the obligations under this Act.
remedies: File formal grievance reports to the company's Data Protection Officer.
Escalate unresolved privacy disputes to the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI).
Keep copies of all communication correspondence logs.

laws.act: Section 8 of the DPDP Act, 2023
laws.summary: Requires companies to maintain database accuracy, secure records, and delete data when no longer needed.
laws.details: The Data Fiduciary is responsible for ensuring the accuracy of processed personal data, implementing reasonable technical security safeguards, and deleting data once the specified purpose is fulfilled.
remedies: File requests to inspect the stored profile details for accuracy.
Demand permanent deletion of your profile history from app databases after account closure.
Report firms lacking firewall security shields to the DPBI.

laws.act: Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Imposes criminal liability and up to 2 years prison for cheque bounces due to insufficient funds.
laws.details: Payee must send a demand notice within 30 days of dishonor. The drawer gets 15 days from notice receipt to pay the amount. Failure to pay within 15 days allows filing a criminal lawsuit within 30 days.
remedies: Settle the bounced cheque amount within 15 days of notice receipt.
Verify if the bank return memo matches account records.
Engage legal counsel to draft a response if cheque was given as security.

laws.act: Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
laws.summary: Presumes that a bounced cheque was issued to discharge a legally enforceable debt.
laws.details: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.
remedies: Gather clear documentation proving the debt was already discharged.
Submit agreements proving the cheque was security and not for active debt.

laws.act: Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.summary: Allows banks to issue 60-day demand notices to default borrowers to clear secured debts.
laws.details: Enables secured creditors (banks) to enforce security interests without court intervention. Banks issue a 60-day demand notice (Sec 13(2)) to the default borrower. If ignored, the bank can take possession.
remedies: Submit formal written objections/representations (Sec 13(3A)) within 15 days.
Pay the overdue balance within 60 days to prevent property possession.
Verify if the asset classification (NPA) matches RBI guidelines.

laws.act: Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.summary: Empowers banks to request Magistrate assistance to take physical control of default properties.
laws.details: Where the possession of any secured asset is required to be taken by the bank, they may request the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or District Magistrate (DM) to take possession.
remedies: Verify if the bank filed a valid affidavit confirming loan terms.
Check if magistrate notice was served to occupants.
File an urgent appeal to stay physical dispossession.

laws.act: Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002
laws.scope: Right to Appeal in Debts Recovery Tribunal
laws.summary: Entitles borrowers to appeal bank enforcement actions within 45 days in the DRT.
laws.details: Any person (including the borrower) aggrieved by bank measures under Section 13(4) may make an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) within forty-five days.
remedies: File a Securitisation Application (SA) in the DRT within 45 days.
Challenge procedural errors in the possession notice.
Obtain an interim stay on property auctions by depositing a fraction of the debt.

laws.act: Section 19 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.summary: Governs formal recovery lawsuits filed by banks in the DRT and defendant reply timelines.
laws.details: Specifies procedures for financial banks to file applications in the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) for debt recovery. The defendant receives summons and must file a Written Statement of defense within 30 days.
remedies: File a detailed Written Reply Statement within 30 days of receiving summons.
Verify interest calculations, compoundings, and penal charges.
File counter-claims if the bank caused monetary losses to your business.

laws.act: Section 20 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.scope: Appeals to Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal
laws.summary: Allows appealing DRT orders to the Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within 30 days.
laws.details: Any person aggrieved by an order made by the DRT may prefer an appeal to the Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) within thirty days from the date of receipt of the order.
remedies: File a formal appeal petition to the DRAT within 30 days.
Submit certified copies of the DRT order.
Deposit the mandatory pre-deposit amount to let the appeal proceed.

laws.act: Section 21 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.scope: Deposit of Debt Amount for Appeal
laws.summary: Mandates pre-depositing 50% of the debt before the DRAT will hear the appeal.
laws.details: No appeal by a debtor shall be entertained by the DRAT unless the debtor deposits fifty percent of the debt amount determined by the DRT. The DRAT may reduce this to not less than twenty-five percent.
remedies: Request a waiver of pre-deposit down to 25% by filing an application.
Pay the pre-deposit amount via demand draft to the DRAT Registry.
Submit arguments of financial hardship to justify a reduced deposit.

laws.act: Section 25 of the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
laws.summary: Details methods Recovery Officers use to recover dues, including selling property or arrest.
laws.details: Allows Recovery Officers to recover the debt specified in the certificate by attachment and sale of movable/immovable property, arrest of the defendant, and appointing a receiver.
remedies: Dispute the attachment of personal properties not mortgaged.
Request installment options to pay off the certificate amount.
Apply to stay arrest warrants by showing cooperative asset disclosures.

laws.act: Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Allows banks to trigger corporate insolvency proceedings in NCLT for loan defaults.
laws.details: A financial creditor (bank/lender) may file an application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) when a default has occurred.
remedies: File a written response disputing the occurrence of default.
Check if the default amount meets the threshold limit (INR 1 Crore).
Settle the outstanding claim through settlement agreements before admission.

laws.act: Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Enables vendors/suppliers to initiate NCLT insolvency after serving a 10-day demand notice.
laws.details: After the expiry of ten days from the delivery of the demand notice under Section 8, if the operational creditor does not receive payment or notice of dispute, they may file an application in the NCLT.
remedies: Serve a reply notice within 10 days highlighting pre-existing quality disputes.
Submit proof of payment transactions.
Settle vendor payments to prevent business insolvency admission.

laws.act: Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016
laws.summary: Declares a freeze on all lawsuits, recovery actions, and foreclosure measures during insolvency.
laws.details: Requires the Adjudicating Authority to declare a moratorium prohibiting: the institution or continuation of suits, enforcement of any security interest (SARFAESI), or recovery of any property.
remedies: Apply to stay active civil court/DRT recovery trials.
Block bank possession notices (Sec 13(4)) while moratorium is active.
Continue operational business transactions under the Resolution Professional.

laws.act: Section 31 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
laws.scope: Submission of Accounts and Balance Sheets
laws.summary: Requires banks to publish audited balance sheets, ensuring public transparency.
laws.details: Mandates that every banking company must prepare and submit audited accounts and balance sheets to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) within three months.
remedies: Request audited financial sheets for corporate loan matching.
Audit bank interest statements against published schedules.
File complaints with the banking ombudsman for illegal accounts manipulations.

laws.act: Section 45ZA of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
laws.summary: Enables bank account holders to nominate individuals to receive deposits upon death.
laws.details: Provides that where a deposit is held by a banking company to the credit of one or more persons, the depositor or, as the case may be, all the depositors together, may nominate one person to whom the deposit may be returned.
remedies: Ensure a nominee is registered for all active bank accounts.
Submit succession/nomination claims to clear deceased account balances.
Verify nominee details in annual bank statement reviews.

laws.act: Section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
laws.scope: Interest Rates Exemption from Usury Laws
laws.summary: Exempts bank loan interest transactions from being reopened under state usury laws.
laws.details: Declares that a transaction between a banking company and its debtor shall not be reopened by any court on the ground that the rate of interest charged by the banking company in respect of such transaction is excessive.
remedies: Verify that your loan interest is calculated using base RBI repo rates.
File grievances if interest rates exceed agreed contract terms.
Audit bank interest statement calculations periodically.

laws.act: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Mandates that a month-to-month lease termination notice must be served in writing with at least 15 days notice.
laws.details: Requires a minimum of 15 days notice for terminating a monthly tenancy of immovable property. The notice must be in writing, signed by the party, and served personally or by post. Failure to provide a full 15-day notice makes any subsequent eviction suit legally void.
remedies: Check the date of service of the eviction notice.
Verify if a full 15 days is allowed before the vacate date.
Consult an advocate to draft a reply highlighting any timing defects.

laws.act: Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.scope: Rights and Liabilities of Landlord and Tenant
laws.summary: Defines mutual rights and duties, including landlord's duty to maintain property and tenant's duty to pay rent.
laws.details: Details that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the landlord is bound to disclose material defects in the property. The tenant is obligated to pay rent at proper times and maintain the property in good condition.
remedies: Request repairs for material property defects.
Keep evidence of regular rent payment transactions.
Send a written notice if the landlord fails to make basic structure repairs.

laws.act: Section 5 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
laws.summary: Allows a person entitled to the possession of specific property to recover it using the Civil Procedure Code (CPC).
laws.details: A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
remedies: File a civil suit for recovery of possession under CPC.
Provide registered sale deed as proof of title ownership.
Apply for interim protection orders to prevent construction by trespassers.

laws.act: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
laws.scope: Suit by Person Dispossessed of Immovable Property
laws.summary: Allows dispossessed persons to recover possession within 6 months without proving title.
laws.details: If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up. Suit must be filed within 6 months.
remedies: File a dispossession lawsuit within 6 months of being forced out.
Gather local police complaint copies proving illegal trespass.
Obtain tenant/neighbor witness statements to prove active possession.

laws.act: Section 7 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882
laws.summary: Protects a landowner's right to enjoy natural advantages of land without interference from neighbors.
laws.details: Each owner of land has the right to enjoy without disturbance by another, the natural advantages arising from its situation, including natural flow of water, light, and air.
remedies: Object to neighbor constructions blocking essential light and air.
File civil injunctions to stop blocking of natural water runoffs.
Apply for structural inspections of shared boundary walls.

laws.act: Section 15 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882
laws.summary: Grants permanent easement rights to access light, air, or way if enjoyed for 20 years without interruption.
laws.details: Where the access and use of light or air, or any way, has been peaceably enjoyed therewith, as an easement, without interruption, and for twenty years, the right becomes absolute.
remedies: Collect evidence of 20 years continuous usage of the pathway.
Register prescriptive easement claims before property transfer.
Dispute neighbor's sudden blockage of historical access gates.

laws.act: Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Defines sale of land and mandates registration for sales exceeding INR 100.
laws.details: Sale is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised. A transfer of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards can be made only by a registered instrument.
remedies: Refuse land purchases based on oral/unregistered agreements.
Register the Sale Deed at the Sub-Registrar office immediately.
Verify non-encumbrance status before executing sale deeds.

laws.act: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Protects a buyer in possession under a written contract even if sale deed is unregistered.
laws.details: Where any person contracts to transfer for consideration any immovable property by writing, and the transferee has taken possession of the property, the transferor cannot evict him.
remedies: Submit the written agreement to sell as defense in eviction suits.
Provide utility bills proving active possession since contract date.
File suits for specific performance to register the final sale deed.

laws.act: Section 18 of the RERA Act, 2016
laws.scope: Return of Amount and Compensation for Delayed Possession
laws.summary: Entitles allottees to a full refund with interest if the promoter fails to give possession on time.
laws.details: Mandates that if the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment in accordance with the agreement for sale, he shall be liable to return the amount received with interest.
remedies: File a claim before the RERA Adjudicating Officer.
Demand refund of principal amount along with prescribed delay interest.
Apply for interest on delay even if you choose to remain in the project.

laws.act: Section 31 of the RERA Act, 2016
laws.summary: Allows any aggrieved person to file a complaint for RERA violations against builders or agents.
laws.details: Provides that any aggrieved person may file a complaint with the RERA Authority or the Adjudicating Officer for any violation or contravention.
remedies: File Form M online on the state RERA portal.
Attach builder agreements and receipt vouchers.
Represent your case personally or via an advocate before the authority.

laws.act: Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Allows a co-owner to sell their share of property, but restricts buyer from occupying a family dwelling house.
laws.details: Where one co-owner of immovable property transfers his share, the transferee acquires the transferor's right. However, if the property is a joint family dwelling house, the buyer does not get joint possession.
remedies: Challenge external buyers attempting to occupy ancestral family homes.
File a partition suit to separate the co-owner's share before transfer.
Obtain co-owner consensus agreements before property leasing.

laws.act: Section 43 of the Land Acquisition Act, 2013
laws.summary: Mandates government to provide rehabilitation packages to families displaced by land acquisition.
laws.details: Requires the Collector to publish a detailed Rehabilitation and Resettlement Award for families whose land is acquired for public purposes, ensuring house and cash compensation.
remedies: Review government acquisition compensation structures.
Submit rehabilitation claims before the land acquisition collector.
File appeals in the Land Acquisition Authority if award is inadequate.

laws.act: Section 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963
laws.scope: Limitation for Suit based on Possession
laws.summary: Sets a 12-year time limit to file lawsuits to recover possession of immovable property.
laws.details: A suit for possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title must be filed within twelve years from the date of dispossession.
remedies: File property recovery suits within the 12-year window.
Track dates of encroachment or illegal occupancy carefully.
Send legal notices immediately on detecting property trespasses.

laws.act: Section 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963
laws.scope: Limitation for Suit based on Title
laws.summary: Sets a 12-year limit for recovering possession based on proprietary title.
laws.details: Limits the recovery of possession based on title to twelve years, running from the date the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
remedies: Take legal action before a squatter completes 12 years of adverse possession.
Pay local property taxes regularly in your name to prove title.
Send warning notices to leaseholder occupants exceeding lease tenures.

laws.act: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
laws.summary: Defines a lease as a transfer of right to enjoy property for a specified time in consideration of price/rent.
laws.details: Establishes that a lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for a certain time, express or implied.
remedies: Ensure the lease document clearly specifies duration.
Verify rent and security deposit refund parameters.
Incorporate lock-in period terms to prevent premature eviction.

laws.act: Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Lists valid legal grounds for seeking divorce, including cruelty, desertion, conversion, and adultery.
laws.details: Specifies grounds upon which a marriage may be dissolved by a decree of divorce, such as: partner treated with cruelty, deserted for not less than two years, ceased to be Hindu by conversion, or had voluntary sexual intercourse with any other person.
remedies: Document instances of cruelty with physical/digital proof.
Draft a comprehensive petition outlining specific matrimonial offenses.
Consult legal counsel to explore family mediation options first.

laws.act: Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Allows couples to seek divorce jointly if living separately for 1 year and unable to live together.
laws.details: Enables divorce by mutual consent. Both parties must file a joint petition stating they have lived separately for a period of one year or more, have not been able to live together, and have mutually agreed to dissolve the marriage.
remedies: Draft a joint settlement agreement for custody and alimony.
File the first motion petition in the Family Court.
Appear for the second motion after the statutory 6-month cooling period (or request waiver).

laws.act: Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 / Sec 144 BNSS
laws.scope: Maintenance of Wives, Children, and Parents
laws.summary: Enables neglected wives, children, and parents to claim monthly maintenance from individuals with sufficient means.
laws.details: Allows a Magistrate of the first class to order a person who possesses sufficient means but neglects or refuses to maintain his wife, children, or parents, to make a monthly allowance for their maintenance.
remedies: File an application for interim maintenance and litigation expenses.
Provide proof of the husband's/child's active income and assets.
Submit proof of your lack of independent income sources.

laws.act: Section 24 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Allows either spouse lacking independent income to claim maintenance and legal costs during divorce trials.
laws.details: Provides that if during matrimonial proceedings, either the wife or the husband has no independent income sufficient for support and expenses, the court may order the other party to pay monthly maintenance and litigation costs.
remedies: File a Section 24 petition during the active divorce suit.
Submit statements of income and standard of living proofs.
Request order execution if spouse fails to pay legal fees.

laws.act: Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Empowers courts to grant permanent monthly or lump-sum alimony to either spouse at the time of decree.
laws.details: Allows the court, while passing any decree under this Act, to order that the respondent shall pay to the applicant for her or his maintenance a gross sum or monthly payment, taking into account income, assets, and conduct of parties.
remedies: File a permanent alimony application along with income affidavits.
Propose a structured lump-sum alimony payment to avoid monthly collections.
Apply to modify the alimony amount if financial circumstances change later.

laws.act: Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Allows a spouse to petition the court to order the other partner to return if they withdrew without reason.
laws.details: When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the District Court, for restitution of conjugal rights.
remedies: File a restitution petition to legally express willingness to reconcile.
Submit proof that the partner left the matrimonial home without valid cause.
Draft defense replies showing partner's cruelty as justification for living apart.

laws.act: Section 12 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Lists grounds to annul voidable marriages, such as impotency, lack of consent by force/fraud, or pre-marriage pregnancy.
laws.details: A marriage may be annulled by a decree of nullity on grounds: that the marriage has not been consummated owing to impotency, that consent was obtained by force or fraud, or that the respondent was pregnant by some other person.
remedies: File an annulment petition within one year of marriage if force/fraud is discovered.
Collect medical certifications for impotency claims.
Cease cohabitation immediately after discovering fraud to protect the annulment suit.

laws.act: Section 26 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
laws.summary: Empowers courts to pass interim and permanent orders for custody, maintenance, and education of minor children.
laws.details: In any proceeding under this Act, the court may pass from time to time interim orders and make provisions in the decree as it may deem just with respect to the custody, maintenance, and education of minor children.
remedies: File an interim child custody and visitation rights petition.
Present proof of child's best welfare interests (schooling, lifestyle).
Apply for court-supervised visitation schedules in family centers.

laws.act: Section 7 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
laws.summary: Authorizes courts to appoint guardians for minor's person or property if it is for the minor's welfare.
laws.details: Where the court is satisfied that it is for the welfare of a minor that an order should be made appointing a guardian of his person or property, the court may make an order accordingly.
remedies: File a guardianship petition in the District Court.
Document the minor's property assets requiring administration.
Provide affidavits showing family support systems for child care.

laws.act: Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
laws.summary: Enables domestic violence victims to apply to Magistrates for protection, residence, and monetary orders.
laws.details: An aggrieved person or a Protection Officer may present an application to the Magistrate seeking reliefs: protection orders (Sec 18), residence orders (Sec 19), monetary relief (Sec 20), or compensation (Sec 22).
remedies: File a DV application detailing instances of domestic abuse.
Request immediate ex-parte interim protection orders from the Magistrate.
Provide proof of shared household residency and income status.

laws.act: Section 18 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
laws.summary: Allows Magistrates to prohibit the respondent from committing acts of violence or entering the victim's workplace.
laws.details: The Magistrate may, after giving the respondent an opportunity of being heard, pass a protection order prohibiting the respondent from committing any act of domestic violence, entering the school/workplace of the victim, or communicating with her.
remedies: Request a restraining order preventing respondent contact.
Submit police complaint receipts showing past domestic threats.
Report breach of protection orders immediately (constitutes a non-bailable offense).

laws.act: Section 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
laws.summary: Protects a victim's right to reside in the shared household and prevents eviction by the partner.
laws.details: Empowers the Magistrate to pass residence orders directing the respondent to: secure alternate accommodation for the victim, remove himself from the shared household, or prohibit him from selling the household.
remedies: Request orders protecting your right to stay in the matrimonial house.
Seek court directions forcing the husband to pay rent for alternate housing.
File objections if the husband attempts to lock you out of the house.

laws.act: Section 20 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
laws.summary: Entitles victims to claim medical expenses, loss of earnings, and monthly maintenance under DV Act.
laws.details: While disposing of an application under section 12, the Magistrate may direct the respondent to pay monetary relief to meet expenses incurred and losses suffered by the victim due to domestic violence, including medical bills and maintenance.
remedies: Submit bills for medical treatments caused by physical abuse.
Provide calculation sheets for monthly household and grocery expenses.
Claim compensation for damage/theft of personal belongings.

laws.act: Section 22 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
laws.summary: Allows Magistrates to order respondents to pay damages for mental torture and emotional distress.
laws.details: The Magistrate may, on an application made by the aggrieved person, pass an order directing the respondent to pay compensation and damages for injuries, including mental torture and emotional distress, caused by domestic violence.
remedies: Claim specific damages for mental harassment during matrimonial stay.
Submit psychologist certificates or treatment records if applicable.
Draft statements detailing emotional abuse and constant threats.

laws.act: Section 18 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956
laws.summary: Entitles a Hindu wife to be maintained by her husband during her lifetime, even if living separately on valid grounds.
laws.details: A Hindu wife shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her life. She is entitled to live separately without forfeiting her claim if the husband is guilty of desertion, cruelty, bigamy, or keeps a concubine.
remedies: File separate maintenance petitions under HAMA.
Establish valid grounds (cruelty/abandonment) for living separately in court.
Submit proof of the husband's family business shares or ancestral earnings.

laws.act: Section 33C of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.scope: Recovery of Money Due from Employer
laws.summary: Allows employees to file claims before the Labor Court to recover unpaid salary, bonus, or gratuity.
laws.details: Provides that where any money is due to a workman from an employer under a settlement or award, the workman may make an application to the Labor Court for recovery of the amount.
remedies: File an application in the Labor Court for recovery of unpaid salary arrears.
Submit bank account statements showing missing salary payments.
Provide copy of employment contract and appointment letters.

laws.act: Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.summary: Prohibits lay-offs/retrenchments unless the worker is given a 1-month notice and severance pay.
laws.details: No workman employed in any industry who has been in continuous service for not less than one year shall be retrenched until: given one month's notice in writing or paid wages in lieu, and retrenchment compensation equal to 15 days' average pay for every year of service.
remedies: Verify if retrenchment compensation is calculated correctly (15 days per year).
Challenge sudden terminations lacking the mandatory 30-day notice period.
File complaints with the regional Labor Commissioner.

laws.act: Section 3 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936
laws.summary: Holds employers directly responsible for paying wages within statutory timeframes (usually by 7th/10th of next month).
laws.details: Every employer shall be responsible for the payment to persons employed by him of all wages required to be paid under this Act. Wages must be cleared before the 7th day (if under 1000 workers) or 10th day.
remedies: Send a written legal notice to HR demanding immediate release of withheld salary.
File complaints before the Inspector under the Payment of Wages Act.
Document daily work logs/emails proving active service during unpaid periods.

laws.act: Section 5 of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
laws.summary: Mandates gratuity pay upon termination/resignation after 5 years continuous service.
laws.details: Gratuity shall be payable to an employee on the termination of his employment after he has rendered continuous service for not less than five years: on superannuation, retirement, or resignation.
remedies: Calculate gratuity amount (15 days wages per year of service).
Submit Form I to the employer within 30 days of leaving.
File an appeal before the Controlling Authority if the employer refuses gratuity clearance.

laws.act: Section 12 of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961
laws.summary: Prohibits employers from discharging or dismissing women employees during maternity leave.
laws.details: When a woman absents herself from work in accordance with the provisions of this Act, it shall be unlawful for her employer to discharge or dismiss her during or on account of such absence.
remedies: File appeals to the Competent Authority within 60 days of wrongful dismissal.
Submit medical certificates proving pregnancy during service.
Claim full maternity wages and additional medical bonuses.

laws.act: Section 4 of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965
laws.scope: Computation of Gross Profits and Bonus
laws.summary: Entitles employees to receive a minimum annual bonus (8.33% of wages) if they worked for 30 days.
laws.details: Every employer shall be bound to pay to every employee who has worked in the establishment for not less than thirty working days in an accounting year, a minimum bonus of 8.33% of the salary earned.
remedies: Verify if the annual bonus calculation matches company profits declarations.
File claims before the Industrial Tribunal if bonus is withheld illegally.
Ensure base eligibility (30 days work) is met.

laws.act: Section 7A of the Employees' Provident Funds Act, 1952
laws.scope: Determination of Moneys Due from Employers
laws.summary: Authorizes PF Commissioners to audit employers and recover unpaid PF contributions.
laws.details: Allows the Central Provident Fund Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner to conduct inquiries to determine the amount due from any employer under the provisions of the Act.
remedies: Check your PF ledger account online using the EPFO portal.
Report employers who deduct PF share from salary but fail to deposit it with EPFO.
Initiate commissioner inquiries for recovery of PF contributions.

laws.act: Section 2(ra) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.summary: Lists illegal employer practices, including victimizing union members or employing workers as temporary casuals.
laws.details: Prohibits employers or workmen from committing any unfair labor practice specified in the Fifth Schedule, such as: discharging workers by way of victimization, or keeping workers temporary to deny permanent benefits.
remedies: File disputes before the labor board for constant temporary contract renewals.
Submit union rosters proving management victimization.
Request inspections of office shift registers and logs.

laws.act: Section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.scope: Dismissal of Workman Deemed Industrial Dispute
laws.summary: Allows individual employees to file cases for wrongful termination without needing a workers union.
laws.details: Where any employer discharges, dismisses, retrenches or otherwise terminates the services of an individual workman, any dispute connected therewith shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute.
remedies: File direct conciliation petitions before the Assistant Labor Commissioner.
Challenge forced resignation letters written under HR coercion.
Demand reinstatement in service with full back wages.

laws.act: Section 9A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.scope: Notice of Change in Service Conditions
laws.summary: Prohibits employers from altering salary, shifts, or leaves without a 21-day notice.
laws.details: No employer who proposes to effect any change in the conditions of service applicable to any workman in respect of wage structure, hours of work, or leave, shall do so without giving 21 days notice.
remedies: Dispute sudden shifts or salary cuts implemented without notice.
File representations before the Conciliation Officer during the 21-day window.
Keep copies of original service agreements.

laws.act: Section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947
laws.summary: Defines industrial disputes as conflicts between employers and workmen regarding employment terms.
laws.details: Establishes that an industrial dispute means any dispute or difference between employers and employers, or between employers and workmen, which is connected with the employment or non-employment.
remedies: Formulate clear demands through registered trade unions.
Refer disputes to industrial tribunals if conciliations fail.
Keep records of charter of demands served to HR.

laws.act: Section 4 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936
